title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The so-called partisan war began with the French entry into Smolensk.

Before partisan warfare was officially recognized by the government, thousands of enemy stragglers, looters, and foragers had already been killed off by Cossacks and peasants, who destroyed them as instinctively as dogs attack a stray rabid dog. Denis Davydov, with his Russian instinct, was the first to recognize the value of this terrible weapon which, heedless of military science's rules, was destroying the French. He deserves the credit for taking the first step toward organizing this method of warfare.
On August twenty-fourth, Davydov's first partisan detachment was formed, and then others were officially recognized. As the campaign progressed, these detachments grew more numerous.

The partisans destroyed the Grand Army piece by piece. They gathered the fallen leaves that dropped by themselves from that withered tree—the French army—and sometimes shook the tree itself. By October, when the French were fleeing toward Smolensk, there were hundreds of such groups, varying widely in size and character. Some adopted full military organization with infantry, artillery, staffs, and amenities. Others consisted solely of Cossack cavalry. There were also small improvised bands of foot and horse, and groups of peasants and landowners that remained unknown. A church sexton commanded one group that captured several hundred prisoners in a month. There was Vasilisa, the wife of a village elder, who killed hundreds of Frenchmen.

The partisan war blazed most fiercely in the final days of October. Its first phase had passed—when the partisans themselves, amazed at their own boldness, feared capture at every moment, hid in the forests without unsaddling, and hardly dared dismount, always expecting pursuit. By late October, this kind of warfare had taken definite shape. Everyone now understood what could and couldn't be risked against the French. Only the commanders of large detachments with staffs, operating at a distance from the French according to established rules, still thought many things impossible. The small bands that had been active from the start and had observed the French up close considered things possible that the big detachment commanders didn't dare contemplate. The Cossacks and peasants who crept in among the French believed everything was possible.

On October twenty-second, Denisov—one of the partisans—was with his band at the height of the guerrilla fervor. Since early morning, he and his men had been on the move. All day he had been watching from the forest alongside the highway a large French convoy of cavalry baggage and Russian prisoners, which—according to spies and captured Frenchmen—was heading for Smolensk under heavy escort, separated from the rest of the army. Besides Denisov and Dolokhov (who also led a small band and operated nearby), the commanders of several large detachments with staffs knew about this convoy too and, as Denisov put it, were 'sharpening their teeth for it.' Two of these commanders—a Pole and a German—sent Denisov near-simultaneous invitations to join forces for an attack on the convoy.

'No, brother, I've grown my own mustache,' said Denisov, reading their messages. He wrote to the German that despite his heartfelt wish to serve under so valiant and famous a general, he had to decline because he was already under the command of the Polish general. To the Polish general, he sent the same reply, informing him he was already under the German's command.

Having arranged things this way, Denisov and Dolokhov planned to attack and seize the convoy on their own, without reporting to the higher command. On October twenty-second, the convoy was moving from the village of Mikulino to Shamshevo. To the left of the road, between Mikulino and Shamshevo, lay large forests that in some places extended right to the road and in others stood a mile or more back. Through these forests, Denisov and his men rode all day, sometimes well inside the tree line, sometimes at the very edge, but never losing sight of the moving French. That morning, Denisov's Cossacks had seized two wagons loaded with cavalry saddles that had gotten stuck in the mud near Mikulino where the forest pressed close to the road. Since then, the party had watched the French column without attacking. They needed to let the French reach Shamshevo undisturbed, and then—after meeting Dolokhov that evening at a watchman's hut in the forest less than a mile from Shamshevo—surprise the French at dawn, falling on them from two sides like an avalanche and routing and capturing them all in one blow.
Behind them, more than a mile from Mikulino where the forest ran right up to the road, six Cossacks were posted to report if any fresh French columns appeared.

Beyond Shamshevo, Dolokhov was watching the road for the same purpose—to find out how far away other French forces were. The convoy was estimated at fifteen hundred men. Denisov had two hundred, and Dolokhov might have as many more. The numerical disadvantage didn't deter Denisov. All he needed to know now was exactly what kind of troops these were, and for that he needed to capture a 'tongue'—that is, take a man from the enemy column. That morning's attack on the wagons had been so hasty that the Frenchmen with them had all been killed. Only a little drummer boy had been taken alive, and since he was a straggler, he could tell them nothing definite about the column's composition.

Denisov thought it too dangerous to make another attack for fear of alerting the entire column. So he sent Tikhon Shcherbaty, a peasant in his band, to Shamshevo to try to grab at least one of the French quartermasters who had been sent ahead.
